newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil ICMS tax cut seen boosting exports four pct.
newsitem.headline: Brazil ICMS tax cut seen boosting exports four pct.

text.p: Removal of a tax on products sold overseas would boost Brazil's overall exports by at least four percent next year and be a boon mainly for soybean, sugar, citrus firms as well as mining, analysts said.
"It's almost a mini-agricultural package," said Ana Cristina Goncalves Costa, an economist with MCM Consultores.
"It would easily raise exports by four percent and maybe more, but the entire economy should benefit," she added.
Congress members this week are expected to take up a bill to exempt exporters of semi-elaborated and primary products from the so-called ICMS tax on sales and services.
Voting to speed the bill through Congress may take place Tuesday, with lawmakers possibly deciding on the measure itself later in the week.
Through the proposal, Brasilia aims to reduce the cost of doing business in Brazil, improve the trade balance and give the economy a badly needed shot in the arm.

Government officials say they have the backing of virtually all states, which stand to lose some 3.6 billion reais in tax revenue next year but will be compensated with relief in their debt to the federal government.
Most analysts agree that the measure is likely to be approved and that its potential impact would be generally positive, especially for raw materials and commodities exporters.
But just how much each would benefit or how the move would impact on product prices is not clear.
"It is an extremely complicated issue," said analyst Eduardo Fornazier of Banco Fator. "You have to look at each company separately."
Analysts said chief beneficiaries will be companies which export iron, soybean, citrus juice and sugar, analysts said.
"For some exporters, the gain from this exemption will amount to an exchange rate devaluation of between four and 20 percent," Fornazier said. He cited the following examples:
* Federal mining giant Cia Vale do Rio Doce would to be exempt from a six percent net duty on 35 million tons of iron ore, gaining $36 million in gross profit in the process.
* Ceval, which exports about $935 million a year in soybean products, should gain $20 million in net profit in 1997 with the rest of the $103 million tax break passed onto soybean producers.
* Souza Cruz would stop paying the equivalent of a 6.5-percent ICMS tax on tobacco, which accounts for 60 percent of its exports, gaining $18 million in gross profits per year.

Analysts said steelmakers Cosipa, Usiminas and Companhia Siderurgica Nacional (CSN) also would benefit. The steel sector as a whole, however, would not see a gain as many firms already receive ICMS-cutting benefits from states.
Apart from shrinking a trade gap threatening to grow to $2 billion this year, the government also hopes Brazil's entire economy will get a long-term boost from the bill.
The measure also would extend the ICMS exemption to purchases of machinery, equipment and goods not directly linked to production, from electrical energy to office equipment.
This aspect of the bill also would help farming, which requires heavy spending on machinery, analysts said.
But, while improving the trade picture through rising exports, the bill also poses an economic risk.
"This is a two-edged sword," one analyst said. "It may help the microeconomic picture but hurt the macroeconomic one by worsening the relationship between tax revenues and public deficit."
-- Sao Paulo newsroom 5511 232 4411
